Siddharth sir ran the Class 10 maths room like an army camp. No talking, no excuses, homework on the desk by 8:05. Shankar had learned more algebra from him in six months than in three years before.
But on Monday, sir cut five marks from Shankar's test because he'd arrived at 8:10. The school bus had broken down on the flyover; half the class had been late. Only Shankar lost marks.
All week Shankar felt torn. He respected sir. He also felt the old burn of resentment every time sir walked past.
On Friday, he waited after class. "Sir, can I say something about Monday?"
"Quickly."
"Your teaching has helped me more than anyone's. But I lost five marks for being late when the bus broke down, and others didn't. That part felt unfair."
Siddharth sir looked at him for a long moment. "Bring me the transport office slip tomorrow," he said. "If it's as you say, I'll fix it."

In Class 11, I asked my chemistry teacher to recheck a practical mark. He leaned over my desk and said quietly, "Complain to anyone and your practical marks will be the lowest in the class, Lalremsiami. Think carefully."
I went cold all over. For three days, I told no one. I kept thinking I was weak for being so scared.
My friend Sabina noticed I'd stopped talking in chemistry. When I told her, she said, "That's a threat. You have to tell your parents today." She walked home with me.
My mother listened, holding my hand. "Being scared doesn't make you weak. It means he frightened you. Write down everything." I wrote the date, his exact words, and who was near us.
That same evening, my father emailed the principal, attaching my notes, and asked for the school's grievance meeting. The principal called back the next morning and set a meeting for Friday.
I still get nervous in that lab. But I'm not silent anymore.

Instead, she took a breath. "Thank you, sir. That means a lot."

Walking home through the Lucknow market, Noor smiled. She'd been right. But what she'd learned was also useful: write things down, stay calm, ask clearly. She'd do the same again.

Leela, come here. I saw you with those boys behind the school wall. Let me tell you what happened to me.
When I was fifteen, in our Indore colony, my friends started bunking tuition to smoke beedis by the railway line. Every evening they'd say, "Come on, Darshan, don't be a scaredy-cat. It's just one."
I wanted to be with them so badly. They were my whole world. For two weeks I made excuses: headache, homework.
Then one evening they surrounded me and held one out. "Now or never."
That was the turning point. I laughed and said, "Never, then," and walked back home along the tracks. My heart was hammering all the way.
They teased me for a month. Then one of them, Sunil, quietly stopped going too. We became closer friends than ever.
Real friends don't make you pay with your health, beta. Your Darshan Chacha learned that by the railway line.

qa.q: Where did young Darshan's friends go to smoke?
qa.a: By the railway line.

qa.q: How did young Darshan feel when his friends pressured him?
qa.a: Young Darshan felt torn and anxious, desperate to belong but not wanting to smoke, his heart hammering as he walked away.

qa.q: What was the turning point, and why did it help?
qa.a: Darshan gave a light but firm no, 'Never, then,' and walked away, which kept him safe and later led Sunil to follow.

qa.q: How might Sunil have felt about Darshan's refusal?
qa.a: Sunil may have admired Darshan's courage and felt freer to stop too.

grounding: Darshan Chacha recalls friends pressuring him to smoke, saying a light but steady no, walking away and finding a truer friend.
